messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Search model from Lee & Wagenmakers, 2014
parts:
I'm trying to understand the intent of these models and not
having much luck. I find it very hard to follow JAGS models
without an idea of what's data and what's a parameter.

Is there a reason you can't just translate the JAGS model line
for line?

- Bob

P.S. I'd suggest recoding this

tmp2[i,q] <- sum(tmp1[i,q,1:nc])
tmp3[i,q] <- -1*step(-tmp2[i,q])+step(tmp2[i,q])
t[i,q] <- tmp3[i,q]+2

but getting rid of the step and replacing it with a conditional.
And you don't need all the indexed temps the way BUGS does. You
can just use local variables. So that'd be:

{
real sum_tmp1_i_q;
sum_tmp1_i_q <- sum(tmp1[i,q]);
if (sum_tmp1_i_q < 0)
t[i,q] <- 1;
else if (sum_tmp1_i_q == 0)
t[i,q] <- 2;
else
t[i,q] <- 3;
}

This makes me think we need a case statement!

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Search model from Lee & Wagenmakers, 2014 [vs. discrete choice model]
parts:
OK --- I read up on the search model, and it's an example of
a model that as stated, isn't going to work well in Stan.

If I understand properly, s is a discrete parameter that can
take on 9! (roughly 350K) values. You'd have to sum those options
out, evaluating each one and then using log_sum_exp().
It might be possible to find a clever dynamic programming algorithm to
reduce the combinatorics, but it'd be a fair amount of work.

How well does the model fit in JAGS or BUGS? I'd think there'd
be a huge problem with multimodality and non-identifiability if
cues are always present or not.

But the real issue is that the take-the-best model (which the search model
generalizes) doesn't seem like it'd give you a very good model of choice.
I'd think different people would know and weight different cues differently
and use more than the first cue in some ordering to decide.

In fact, I'd suggest trying a discrete choice model of the sort
used by economists ( http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_choice ).

Each choice gets a predictor vector indicating with values corresponding
to 1 for cues that are "on" and 0 for those that are "off".

Then each subject has a coefficient vector. They then choose an item with
probabilities given by softmax (aka multinomial logistic regression).

For example, if choice a has predictor vector x_a and b has predictor vector x_b,
and the coefficient vector for choices is beta, then

Pr[choice = a] = exp(beta * x_a) / ( exp(beta * x_a) + exp(beta * x_b) )

This generalizes naturally to more than two choices.

If a cue is the same for all choices, it drops out. If a
cue has a very large coefficient, it will dominate anything
smaller if anything larger cancels out. So I'd think if the
take-the-best structure is there, you'd see it emerge in the
coefficients.

Then you can use one coefficient vector (complete pooling), give
each subject their own independent vector (no pooling), or build
a hierarchical model to estimate the amount of partial pooling to apply.

An added bonus is that a discrete choice model should be
easy to fit in Stan :-)

- Bob

Bob, thank you for getting to it and for your suggestions, I'll forward your answer to E.J.. 

Jags and BUGS seems to fit the model well, but I didn't inspect it deeply. 

Yes, that TTB model is not well describing the data, but I think it was meant to be like that. TTB is oversimplified, the next model (Stopping) introduces different way to process the cues - Weighted Additive model, which improves the fit of the data. Then third model is trying to improve TTB and the fourth is combining second and third model into something better.   

Thanks again.
Martin
